claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by in situ formation of a protective, adherent tribo-oxide layer during sliding.
The tribo-oxide reduces friction and wear by acting as a self-healing barrier that prevents direct asperity contact.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a typical nanocrystalline or amorphous microstructure.
The as-deposited coating surface is largely oxide-free.
An oxygen-rich environment during high-temperature sliding will promote in situ oxidation relative to an inert or low-oxygen environment.
Sliding at 400–600 °C with controlled oxygen partial pressure can produce consistent oxide formation.
High-temperature wear produces a nanostructured, adherent, and lubricious tribo-oxide scale on the coating surface.
At elevated temperature, oxygen diffuses into the coating surface during sliding and triggers rapid oxidation.
The resulting oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and lowers friction.
Reduced contact and friction mitigate plastic deformation and material removal, thereby increasing wear resistance.
Compared with inert testing, oxygen-rich testing will produce a discernible, continuous tribo-oxide layer.
Compared with inert testing, oxygen-rich testing will increase coating surface hardness.
Compared with inert testing, oxygen-rich testing will lower the friction coefficient.
Compared with inert testing, oxygen-rich testing will significantly reduce the wear rate.
Minimal in situ oxidation occurs during baseline wear testing in an inert or low-oxygen atmosphere.
The proposed protective-oxide mechanism is effective between 400 and 600 °C under cyclic sliding loads typical of high-temperature applications.
Outside the stated temperature and loading limits, oxidation kinetics or mechanical loading may not favor formation or stabilization of the protective oxide.
